revenue.definition: All the money a company takes in from selling its products and services, before paying any costs. Also called sales.

net-income.definition: The profit left after paying every cost, including wages, interest and taxes. Often called the bottom line.

net-loss.definition: When a company's costs, including interest and taxes, add up to more than it earned during the period.

gross-margin.definition: The share of each dollar of sales left after paying the direct cost of making or buying what was sold. Higher means more is left for everything else.

profit-margin.definition: The share of each dollar of sales left as profit after all costs and taxes.

operating-income.definition: Profit from the company's main business, before interest and taxes.

cash-from-operations.definition: The cash the company's everyday business actually brought in during the period. It can differ from profit because of timing, such as customers paying later.

cash-and-equivalents.definition: Money in the bank plus very safe investments that can be turned into cash almost immediately.

long-term-debt.definition: Money the company has borrowed and must pay back over more than a year, such as bonds and bank loans.

quarter.definition: A three-month period. US public companies report their results every quarter.

fiscal-year.definition: The 12-month period a company uses for its accounts. It doesn't have to match the calendar year; Apple's ends in late September, for example.

10-k.definition: The detailed yearly report US public companies must file with the SEC. It covers the business, its risks and audited financial statements.

10-q.definition: The report US public companies file with the SEC for each of the first three quarters of their year. It is shorter than the annual report and not fully audited.

8-k.definition: A filing companies make with the SEC within days of a major event, such as results, a new chief executive or a big acquisition.

sec.definition: The US Securities and Exchange Commission, the government agency that oversees stock markets and collects company filings.

risk-factors.definition: The section of a report where the company lists the things that could hurt its business or its share price.

operating-margin.definition: The share of each dollar of sales left as profit from the main business, before interest and taxes.

eps.definition: The company's profit divided by the number of its shares. "Diluted" counts shares that could be created later, for example from employee stock awards.

free-cash-flow.definition: The cash the business brought in, minus what it spent on buildings, equipment and other long-term investments. It shows how much spare cash the company produced.

capital-expenditure.definition: Money spent on long-lasting things like factories, stores, data centres and equipment. Also called capital expenditure or capex.

current-ratio.definition: Short-term assets (cash and things expected to turn into cash within a year) divided by bills due within a year. Above 1 means it has more than enough to cover them.

debt-to-equity.definition: How much the company has borrowed compared with the money that belongs to its shareholders. Higher means it relies more on borrowing.

shareholders-equity.definition: What would be left for shareholders if the company sold everything it owns and paid off everything it owes, based on its accounts.

return-on-equity.definition: A year's profit divided by shareholders' equity. It shows how much profit the company made with the money that belongs to its shareholders.

assets.definition: Everything the company owns that has value: cash, buildings, equipment, money owed to it, and more.

total-liabilities.definition: Everything the company owes: loans, bonds, bills to suppliers, taxes due, and other obligations.

share-buyback.definition: When a company buys its own shares from the market. It leaves fewer shares, so each remaining share owns a bigger slice of the company.

dividend.definition: Cash a company pays out to its shareholders, usually every quarter, from its profits.

auditor.definition: An independent accounting firm that checks a company's financial statements every year and says whether they are fairly presented.

restatement.definition: A filing where a company says financial statements it published earlier contained errors and should no longer be relied on.

pe-ratio.definition: The share price divided by earnings per share. It shows how many dollars investors are paying for each dollar of yearly profit. It describes the price; it doesn't say whether the price is right.

market-cap.definition: The share price multiplied by the number of shares: what the whole company is worth on the stock market at that moment.

share-price.definition: What one share of the company costs on the stock market. It moves every trading day as people buy and sell.
